# Chapter 15 - sketch answers {.unnumbered}

\(1\) (a) Standard - specific, mandatory, measurable. (b) Policy -
high-level intent and direction. (c) Guideline - recommended, judgement-based,
not mandatory. (d) Procedure - step-by-step how. (2) Policy: "We can recover
our data and services after loss." Standard: Nightly encrypted backups, 30-day
retention, quarterly restore test. Procedure: The restore checklist, step by
step, from console to verification. Guideline: Tips for choosing what else
(laptops, shared drives) is worth backing up. (3) Design: The
access/authentication standard (and the policy above it). Operation: The MFA
configuration export, and authentication logs or the periodic access-review
sign-off. Design without operation means a paper control - designed, not
operating - which an auditor reports as ineffective (Chapter 10's ineffective
control, found by Chapter 16's method). (4) Finding: The incident-response
documentation is outdated and diverges from actual practice, so the documented
control no longer matches reality. Risk: In an incident, staff follow an
outdated or private procedure - exploiting the unmaintained documentation -
so that response is delayed and inconsistent, extending the outage and its cost.
(5) Pillar 1: The documented ICT risk framework, board minutes showing
accountability. Pillar 2: The incident classification scheme and a filed
major-incident report template. Pillar 3: The testing plan and last test's
evidence (TLPT only if designated significant). Pillar 4: The register of
information listing every ICT contract. Pillar 5: Membership or participation
record in an intelligence-sharing arrangement. For merchants: Indirectly yes -
expect revised contracts with notification duties and cooperation clauses,
because our compliance now depends partly on you.
